body:
Producing more value with fewer resources

Resource efficiency means obtaining greater useful output or human benefit from a given quantity of resources, or providing the same benefit while using fewer resources and creating fewer harmful environmental effects.

Resources involved may include water, land, energy, minerals, biomass and other materials. Resource efficiency applies not only to factories but also to farming, households, transport, construction and public services.

For example, improving irrigation can allow farmers to produce crops with less water. Better building design can provide acceptable indoor conditions with less energy use. Repairing an appliance can extend its useful life and reduce the demand for new materials.

Efficiency is not identical to conservation

Resource conservation seeks to protect resources from unnecessary depletion or degradation. Resource efficiency concerns the relationship between useful output and resource input. Efficient use can contribute to conservation, but the 2 are not identical.

A factory may reduce the amount of water needed per product while increasing total production so much that its total water withdrawal rises. Therefore, lower resource use per unit of output does not necessarily mean lower total resource use.

A simple example

Suppose a factory initially manufactures 100 products using 1,000 litres of water. After introducing more efficient machinery, it manufactures the same 100 products using 800 litres. Water use per product has fallen from 10 litres to 8 litres, a reduction of 20%.

If the factory subsequently doubles production to 200 products at the new efficiency level, it uses 1,600 litres. Water efficiency has improved, but total water use is now higher than the original 1,000 litres.

If the efficiency improvement causes the increase in production, this illustrates the rebound effect: efficiency improvements can lower the cost of using a resource and encourage increased activity or consumption that offsets some of the expected savings.

Resource use and economic growth

Decoupling refers to weakening or breaking the link between economic activity and resource use or environmental damage.

  • Relative decoupling: Resource use or environmental pressure grows more slowly than economic output. The quantity used per unit of output falls, but total resource use may still rise.
  • Absolute decoupling: Total resource use or the relevant environmental pressure decreases while economic output grows.

The distinction is important because an improvement in resource productivity does not necessarily establish that the total pressure on nature is declining.

Renewable and non-renewable resources

Renewable resources can be replenished through natural processes, but only under suitable conditions and within relevant time periods. Forests, fisheries and groundwater require careful management because extraction can exceed their renewal or recharge rates.

Non-renewable resources, such as coal and petroleum, are formed over geological time and cannot be replenished within ordinary human time scales. Their sustainable management therefore places importance on reducing waste, improving efficiency, recovering usable materials where possible, developing alternatives and limiting harmful environmental effects.

For a renewable resource, extraction that persistently exceeds regeneration can cause depletion. For a non-renewable resource, efficient use may slow depletion but does not make the resource renewable.

Practical approaches to resource efficiency

  • Reduce: Prevent unnecessary use of energy, water and materials.
  • Reuse: Use products or materials again where safe and appropriate.
  • Repair: Extend the life of useful products instead of replacing them prematurely.
  • Recycle: Recover useful materials from discarded products, recognizing that recycling also requires energy and may involve material losses.
  • Improve processes: Reduce leakage, waste generation and avoidable losses during production and distribution.

These approaches support a circular economy, which seeks to keep products and materials useful for longer and reduce waste. However, circular practices do not eliminate the need to control total resource demand or protect ecosystems.

Connections with the SDGs

Resource efficiency is particularly relevant to SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production. Target 12.2 concerns the sustainable management and efficient use of natural resources by 2030.

Water-use efficiency is also addressed under SDG 6. Target 6.4 aims to substantially increase water-use efficiency across sectors while addressing sustainable withdrawals, freshwater supply and water scarcity.

Efficient use and sustainable withdrawal must be considered together. A water-saving technology may be beneficial, but the condition of a river or aquifer depends on the total amount withdrawn and the availability of water for people and ecosystems.

Prelims focus

  • Resource efficiency concerns useful output or benefit relative to resource input.
  • Relative decoupling does not necessarily mean an absolute reduction in resource use.
  • Absolute decoupling involves declining total resource use or environmental pressure alongside growing economic output.
  • SDG Target 12.2 concerns sustainable management and efficient use of natural resources.
  • SDG Target 6.4 concerns water-use efficiency and sustainable freshwater withdrawals.
  • Trap: A renewable resource can still be depleted when extraction exceeds regeneration.

[United Nations Environment Programme, International Resource Panel, Global Resources Outlook 2024, Glossary entries on resource efficiency and resource decoupling; NCERT, Class 8, Resources and Development, Chapter 1, Resources; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 172–175; United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, SDG 6, Target 6.4, and SDG 12, Target 12.2, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Lower resource use per product does not always reduce total resource consumption.

title: Resource Efficiency and the Sustainable Use of Natural Resources

body:
Why ecological limits matter

The Earth contains interacting systems that regulate climate, water circulation, nutrient cycles and the conditions necessary for life. Human activities can place increasing pressure on these systems through pollution, land conversion, resource extraction and greenhouse-gas emissions.

The planetary boundaries framework identifies 9 major Earth-system processes and considers the limits within which humanity can operate while reducing the risk of large-scale and potentially irreversible environmental change.

The framework was first proposed in 2009 by an international research team led by Johan Rockström. It provides a scientific way of thinking about the Earth's safe operating space.

The 9 planetary boundaries

  1. Climate change: Disturbance of the Earth's climate system through rising greenhouse-gas concentrations and related changes.
  2. Biosphere integrity: Loss of biodiversity and weakening of the ecological functions performed by living organisms.
  3. Land-system change: Conversion and alteration of natural landscapes, including the replacement of forests by other forms of land use.
  4. Freshwater change: Disturbance of freshwater systems and water availability, including changes affecting rivers, groundwater and soil moisture.
  5. Biogeochemical flows: Disruption of major nutrient cycles, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, including through excessive nutrient releases.
  6. Ocean acidification: Changes in ocean chemistry associated with the absorption of carbon dioxide.
  7. Stratospheric ozone depletion: Reduction of the protective ozone layer in the stratosphere.
  8. Atmospheric aerosol loading: Changes in atmospheric particles that can affect climate, rainfall and environmental conditions.
  9. Novel entities: Introduction and accumulation of substances or other entities, including synthetic chemicals and plastics, that can create environmental risks.

What happens when a boundary is crossed?

Exceeding a planetary boundary indicates that humanity has moved beyond the assessed safe operating space for that Earth-system process. It means that the risk of undesirable environmental change has increased.

Crossing a boundary does not necessarily mean that an environmental disaster occurs immediately or that every effect is irreversible. The framework identifies increasing risks, and different Earth-system processes respond in different ways.

The boundaries are also interconnected. For example, converting forests into other land uses can affect biodiversity, carbon storage and water circulation. Excessive nitrogen and phosphorus flows can contribute to deterioration of water quality and aquatic ecosystems.

Status in the 2026 scientific assessment

The Planetary Health Check 2026, published by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research on 21 September 2026, assessed that 7 of the 9 planetary boundaries had been transgressed.

The 7 boundaries identified as transgressed were climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification and novel entities.

The assessment did not classify stratospheric ozone depletion and atmospheric aerosol loading as globally transgressed. However, this does not mean that these processes present no environmental concerns. In particular, unsafe aerosol conditions can still occur in individual regions.

The number of planetary boundaries classified as transgressed is a scientific assessment that can change when new evidence, methods or updated measurements become available. The 7-of-9 result refers specifically to the assessment published on 21 September 2026, using the latest available scientific data, some of which predate 2026.

Planetary boundaries and the SDGs are not the same framework

The planetary boundaries framework is primarily a scientific assessment of Earth-system stability. The Sustainable Development Goals are internationally agreed development objectives that include poverty, health, education, economic opportunities, governance and environmental protection.

Consequently, the 9 planetary boundaries must not be confused with the 17 SDGs. The 2 frameworks are related because environmental stability supports human development, but their purposes and structures differ.

Planetary boundaries also help explain strong sustainability. If an ecological function is essential and difficult to replace, development decisions must take its limits seriously rather than assume that economic investment can compensate for all damage.

Prelims focus

  • The planetary boundaries framework identifies 9 major Earth-system processes.
  • It was first proposed in 2009 by a research team led by Johan Rockström.
  • The Planetary Health Check dated 21 September 2026 assessed 7 of 9 boundaries as transgressed.
  • Ocean acidification was among the transgressed boundaries in that assessment.
  • Stratospheric ozone depletion and atmospheric aerosol loading were not classified as globally transgressed in the 2026 assessment.
  • Trap: Boundary transgression indicates increased risk, not necessarily immediate or certain ecological collapse.

[Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, Planetary Health Check 2026: A Scientific Assessment of the State of the Planet, published 21 September 2026, DOI 10.48485/pik.2026.25, overview and boundary assessments; Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, news release, Planetary Health Check 2026 finds mounting pressures across Earth's life support systems, 21 September 2026; European Environment Agency, Exiting the Anthropocene? Exploring fundamental change in our relationship with nature, discussion of ecological limits, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The 2026 assessment marks 7 of 9 boundaries as transgressed; ozone depletion and aerosol loading are not classified as globally transgressed.
pictures.caption: The 2026 assessment identified 7 transgressed planetary boundaries out of 9.

title: Planetary Boundaries and the Safe Operating Space for Humanity

body:
How the global development framework evolved

International cooperation on sustainable development developed through several important milestones.

  • 1987: The Brundtland Commission published Our Common Future, establishing the widely used definition of sustainable development.
  • 1992: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, commonly called the Earth Summit, was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It adopted Agenda 21, a programme of action for sustainable development.
  • 2000: The United Nations Millennium Declaration formed part of the foundation for the Millennium Development Goals, or MDGs. The MDG framework contained 8 goals with a 2015 target horizon.
  • 2012: The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, known as Rio+20, helped advance the process for establishing Sustainable Development Goals.
  • 25 September 2015: The United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 70/1, Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
  • 1 January 2016: The 2030 Agenda's implementation period began.
  • 2030: The overall target year for the Agenda, although some individual targets have earlier deadlines.

What the SDGs are

The Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs, are 17 integrated global goals supported by 169 targets. They seek to advance human well-being, economic opportunity, social inclusion, peace and environmental protection.

The SDGs apply to all countries, developed and developing alike. They are universal, but the 2030 Agenda recognizes differences in national circumstances, capacities, priorities and levels of development.

The goals are internationally agreed commitments rather than a treaty creating automatic legal penalties for countries that do not achieve a target. Implementation depends on national policies, institutions, resources and cooperation.

The names and central concerns of all 17 goals

SDGOfficial short nameCentral concern
1No PovertyEnd poverty in all its forms.
2Zero HungerEnd hunger and improve food security and nutrition.
3Good Health and Well-beingPromote health and well-being for all.
4Quality EducationEnsure inclusive and equitable quality education.
5Gender EqualityAchieve gender equality and empower women and girls.
6Clean Water and SanitationEnsure sustainable access to water and sanitation.
7Affordable and Clean EnergyImprove access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy.
8Decent Work and Economic GrowthPromote inclusive economic growth and decent employment.
9Industry, Innovation and InfrastructureBuild resilient infrastructure and support sustainable industry and innovation.
10Reduced InequalitiesReduce inequality within and among countries.
11Sustainable Cities and CommunitiesMake settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable.
12Responsible Consumption and ProductionPromote sustainable consumption and production patterns.
13Climate ActionTake urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts.
14Life Below WaterConserve and sustainably use oceans and marine resources.
15Life on LandProtect and restore terrestrial ecosystems and biodiversity.
16Peace, Justice and Strong InstitutionsPromote peaceful, inclusive societies and accountable institutions.
17Partnerships for the GoalsStrengthen implementation and global partnerships.

The 5 Ps of sustainable development

The Preamble of the 2030 Agenda organizes its broad vision around 5 Ps:

  • People: End poverty and hunger and enable people to live in dignity, equality and a healthy environment.
  • Planet: Protect natural resources and the environment from degradation.
  • Prosperity: Promote fulfilling lives and economic progress in harmony with nature.
  • Peace: Build peaceful, just and inclusive societies.
  • Partnership: Mobilize cooperation and resources to achieve the Agenda.

The 5 Ps describe the Agenda's broad areas of action. They are not 5 additional SDGs, and they should not be treated as completely separate groups. A single goal can contribute to several of these areas.

How the SDGs differ from the MDGs

The MDGs concentrated strongly on poverty reduction and selected human-development outcomes. The SDGs build on that earlier framework but address a wider range of issues, including sustainable consumption, climate, biodiversity, inequality, infrastructure, institutions and international partnerships.

The SDGs also apply explicitly to all countries, not only to problems primarily associated with developing countries.

Agenda 21 was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. The 2030 Agenda containing the 17 SDGs was adopted in 2015. Their names are similar, but they are different documents adopted at different times.

Prelims focus

  • The SDGs were adopted on 25 September 2015 through UN General Assembly Resolution 70/1.
  • There are 17 SDGs and 169 targets.
  • The 2030 Agenda took effect on 1 January 2016.
  • The 5 Ps are People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership.
  • SDG 16 concerns peace, justice and strong institutions; SDG 17 concerns partnerships and implementation.
  • Trap: The SDGs are universal goals, not goals intended only for developing countries.

[United Nations General Assembly, Resolution 70/1, Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted 25 September 2015, Preamble, Declaration and Goals and Targets; United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, official Sustainable Development Goals pages, consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Class 10, Contemporary India II, Chapter 1, Resources and Development, discussion of the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and Agenda 21; World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (1987), Chapter 2.]
